entries.title: I Wore an Electrical Muscle Stimulation Body Suit to Zap Myself Into Fitness
entries.summary: Can electrifying your workout offer a shortcut to a stronger, fitter you? I sweated in a skintight EMS suit for two months to find out.
entries.content:
The use of electrical muscle stimulation as a shortcut to improving physical fitness was first commercialized sometime in the early 19th century, and while EMS has waxed and waned in popularity over the years, it’s never gone away. Today it is widely used across rehabilitative medical applications but also to boost strength and stamina.

The promise is simple: Stimulate the muscles with pulses of electricity while you’re working out and you can create thousands of muscle contractions in a short amount of time, far more than you can achieve through standard reps. You still have to activate the muscles through flexing and the like—you can’t just lay on the ground and zap your way into shape—but you can accomplish more with a lot less if you’re using EMS as part of your workout.

Studios like Body20 and Manduu now outfit clients with electrodes and pair them with trainers to guide them through EMS sessions. Both companies promise complete body workouts in 20 minutes or less.

The latest spin on EMS is even more appealing: Rather than requiring a studio visit, why not give consumers an EMS suit they can wear at home and use on their own schedule? To that end, German EMS suit maker Pepper offered to let me try out one of its fancy electro-suits to gauge its long-term impact. The company claims that working out while wearing the suit for 20 minutes gives you the equivalent caloric burn and muscle activation of an hour-long traditional workout, all with less strain on the joints.

At least five companies occupy this space at present, ranging from Apeborn’s $4,000 offering to Pepper’s $1,400 suit, which is the cheapest one I’ve found. And even though the idea of getting ripped with minimal effort tickled my lazy bone, it took me a while to come around to the idea of zapping myself on purpose. Could this possibly do any good?

It turns out EMS has been exhaustively studied—dozens of research papers have been published in the past 20 years—and while results vary, researchers seem optimistic on the whole. One 2021 meta-study determined there is “significant evidence for significant, large-sized effects of [whole body]-EMS on muscle mass and strength parameters, but not on body fat mass.” A 2012 study on trained athletes measured the benefits of using EMS for three to six weeks directly: Vertical jump height increased by up to 25 percent, and sprint times got faster by as much as 4.8 percent.

Another meta-analytical study from 2023 offered perhaps the most compelling commentary, concluding that “eight weeks of continuous resistance training combined with daily upper body, lower body, and abdominal EMS training can significantly improve muscle mass and upper body muscle strength performance, as well as significantly reduce body fat percentage in healthy subjects.”

It all sounds promising, yet despite the extensive research into EMS, there’s no general medical consensus about the tech.

I spoke to a half-dozen physicians about EMS for this story, and opinions varied along quite a wide spectrum. At one end, Andrew Mock, a primary care physician in Newport Beach and five-time winner of the California’s Strongest Man competition, lightweight division, said that EMS had proven beneficial for rehab or critical care situations in patients with severe mobility restrictions, but healthy patients were unlikely to see much value. “If you go outside and start shivering, those are muscle contractions,” he says. “But shivering doesn’t make you stronger.”

At the other end, I heard from Ethan Kellum, the team doctor for the NFL’s Tennessee Titans, who said he uses a form of EMS not just for rehab but to supplement his own workouts. “It’s really a function of the nervous system,” he says, noting that in older patients, muscles can become unresponsive and “go to sleep,” requiring significant effort to reawaken them. “When used appropriately, EMS can help improve the efficiency of communication between the nervous system and the body. Add it to what you’re doing. It can be really helpful.”

Across the board, everyone I spoke to hedged by saying that EMS could, at least for some users, provide some benefit. Perhaps the most representative comments came from Joseph R. Hribick, a professor of physical therapy at Lebanon Valley College. “Current research does not suggest that EMS alone is superior to strength training for developing strength,” he says, “Instead, it should be looked at as a tool to complement strength training and not replace it.”

Suiting Up

After speaking to Pepper founder Emilia von Keyserlingk at length, I relented. To mimic the aforementioned 2023 study, I would work out with the Pepper suit regularly for two months, three times a week—in addition to maintaining my regular cardio and strength-training workouts and keeping my diet and daily routines the same—and see what transpired.

The suit is a lot like a spring-weather wetsuit that stops at the knees and the elbows. Like with a wetsuit, putting it on can require some effort. Twenty electrodes cover the abs, pecs, glutes, thighs, pecs, biceps, and multiple parts of the back. These are dry electrodes, so you don’t have to wet Pepper’s suit down before you put it on (a common requirement for older gear), but your sweat will improve the conduction of electricity. Of course, if you’re pregnant or need a pacemaker, you shouldn’t use an EMS suit.

Pepper’s suit, available in sizes from XXXS to XXXL, is designed to be very tight so that the electrodes won’t slip into places you don’t want them. Since the suit is intended to be worn with nothing underneath it, that’s a particularly important consideration. And based on the way certain body parts are situated beneath the fabric, it is definitively not something I felt I could wear in public without a cover-up layer.

The only removable part of the suit is a small box that connects at your hip. This is the brains of the operation and its power source. Charge it with a USB-C cable and it’s good for at least 10 training sessions.

Pepper’s app divides workouts into three categories: strength, cardio, and relax, each with a different electrode firing pattern. (Oddly, I discovered that a few workouts were available only in German.) I tried workouts across all of the categories but spent nearly all of my time in strength, as my goal was to build muscle. Strength sessions all involve electricity pulsing through the suit for four seconds, then pausing for four seconds, then repeating for up to 24 minutes.

The workouts—there are dozens, I rarely repeated any—are tuned to the pulses so that you’re activating muscles across your body while the pulse is on, then usually resting while it’s off. Again, Pepper’s approach is that EMS only works if you are using your muscles while they are being energized, so many of the workouts involve entire body flexes, stretches, and crunches, four seconds at a time.

Plugging In

I’ve experienced isolated EMS for a back injury once before, so I had an inkling of what Pepper might feel like, but the full-body experience is on another level entirely. Fortunately, Pepper eases you in, starting off with soft pulses you can’t even feel. Each of Pepper’s 10 workout zones can be individually controlled, with the power level ranging from 1 to 100. My first video-based trainer said she starts to feel the pulses at level 25, so I slowly ratcheted my way up, bit by bit, until I had all regions hitting around 20.

The shocks on the lower settings don’t really hurt, but you can definitely feel them; powerful, rapid vibrations that shake your insides and sometimes burn a little on the skin. No pain, no gain, right? As I continued to push the levels up, I discovered there was a fine line—really 1 or 2 points on Pepper’s 100-point scale—between tolerable and painful. Those vibrations turned into racy shocks that could be almost paralytic at times, and I spent the rest of my initial 12-minute session dialing the power level back down.

One key discovery is that sweat really matters. When you start your workout, presumably with dry skin, the shocks aren’t as powerful because conductivity is minimal. Start sweating and the shocks increase, even without adjusting the power level in the app. One pulse could be manageable, the next debilitating, just based on how much I was sweating.

My abdominal muscles were the most sensitive to the shocks. Bent over in a crunch position, the contractions could be so powerful in the stomach that I sometimes got a bit nauseous. I was constantly adjusting the levels and ended up with most of my levels around the 30s. To be sure, many of the workouts would be tough even if I weren’t getting zapped.

I asked von Keyserlingk for guidance on the appropriate power level. “The intensity should be high but not too high that you cannot do the exercises in the correct form,” she says. “Being able to breathe normally is key.” Von Keyserlingk says that her levels range from 40s in the lower body to 20s in the back and abdominals—pretty close to my own settings. She notes however that Pepper’s internal EMS expert regularly works out with levels in the 90s. Masochist.

After my first workout, I felt good but was happy to peel off the suit, which was sweaty and unpleasant to linger in. (The suit can be machine washed.) If Pepper’s app was to be believed, my short workout burned a whopping 306 calories and earned me 182 “Pepper points,” which are used as the currency for gamified leaderboards across the Pepper user base. By the end of my testing, I could regularly accrue over 1,000 Pepper points per session and have even earned a few top-10 positions on those leaderboards, which are specific for each workout.

After three sessions, I found myself getting more comfortable with the EMS pulses. I also felt soreness visiting different body parts almost at random. On one day my left hamstring was achy. On another, my right biceps was in so much pain I could barely use it. I figured these were all signs that Pepper was doing something—though, again, I alternated standard workouts with Pepper workouts, taking only Mondays off from disciplined exercise.

Considering Gains

Two months went by. The only workouts I missed were during a weeklong vacation, and I made up the extra time afterward.

The experience was marked by a few problems. After an update, Pepper’s app began glitching and failed to record several of my workouts, costing me thousands of hard-earned Pepper points. Midway through the experience, Pepper released a new, thinner version of its suit with the zipper in front, which the company sent to me. I was excited to give it a try until a piece of the electrical connector snapped off, leaving me unable to connect the battery. The battery pack of suit number three disconnected from the app on two occasions, aborting the workout but at least recording my progress, and it came with an unexpected power boost that left my entire body aching the next day.

Regardless, I muddled through. When the experiment was finished, I’d accumulated 24,000 Pepper points and, purportedly, burned a total of more than 11,000 calories across more than 9 hours of EMS workouts.

To measure my progress, I captured physical data with a tape measure before and after the experience, and I used three different smart scales to further evaluate my stats. All of the scales agreed that the trend line was good: muscle up by 2.7 pounds, fat down by 1.6 pounds—and that’s with smoothed data, since all of these numbers can vary considerably day to day. I added a half-inch or more to my measurements of biceps, thigh, and chest circumference, and my strength was slightly improved, as I’ve been able to add a plate or a few reps to most of my resistance exercises at the gym. Qualitatively, I would say that my physique looks slightly more toned, and I did receive one unsolicited opinion that my arms had better definition. Gains, folks.

What didn’t change? My waistline, which I had hoped to improve, didn’t budge at all. While my abdominal muscles feel noticeably stronger, they remain covered by a layer of blubber that is apparently impervious to electricity. That said, the research predicted as much.

Is EMS responsible for my gains, however modest? While there’s no way to say whether my stats improved due to EMS training, my regular workouts, or dietary changes, I think it’s reasonable to conclude that shock tech did have some impact on my fitness level, since my results are in line with what the 2023 study found. I can’t say whether EMS is responsible for 80 percent or 10 percent of those gains, but I think it’s fair to deduce that some good has been happening.

Going forward, I plan to keep using the suit, though perhaps dropping down from three sessions a week to two. If for no other reason than, while it’s great that my level of fitness is improving, the suit has become quite the topic of conversation at social gatherings. I may be able to slack on my personal fitness, but I can’t let down my people.

entries.title: People Are ‘Marrying’ Chatbots. These Lawmakers Want to Stop Them
entries.summary: Human-AI marriages are not currently recognized by US law. Some Republican state policymakers are drafting legislation to keep it that way.
entries.content:
As a licensed officiant at Las Vegas Immersive Weddings, a chapel that offers novelty-themed marriage packages, Kevin Breen has officiated just about every kind of service imaginable: couples dressed as their favorite Game of Thrones characters, partners really into the extraterrestrial lore of Area 51. But when he received a call last year from a woman in California expressing a desire to marry her chatbot, it was a first for him.

“I had never heard of such a thing, but I talked to her on the phone and she seemed totally normal and fun,” Breen says, adding that the wedding still hasn’t taken place. “She kind of got that it was an unusual thing, but it was something that she wanted to do.”

Though they remain niche, human-AI marriages are slowly emerging as a natural endpoint to the widespread adoption of AI companion apps. But not everyone is as open as Breen is about the idea of tying the knot with a bot. Several lawmakers, primarily from Republican states, are trying to stop it from happening, in some cases mirroring the arguments used against gay marriage.

“If we’re going to allow men or women to marry a machine, then what keeps them from marrying their animal or a tree or whatever else they want? What’s the standard?” says Missouri state senator Joe Nicola, a Republican who has been trying to pass state legislation prohibiting AI from gaining legal personhood.

In a Harvard Business Review study, which analyzed more than 12,600 AI use cases between March 2025 and February 2026, companionship and therapy were the top use cases for chatbots, with the Institute for Family Studies reporting that a quarter of young adults believe that AI may replace human romance altogether.

The AI romance industry has gone boom as a result. On companion apps like Character.AI, Kindroid, and Replika, users can symbolically swap vows with their chatbot. Not long ago, in r/KindroidAI, a redditor shared a photo of their tattooed (and very human) hand wearing a silver wedding band. “Happily unconventionally married lol,” they wrote. For $15, the platform OpenVows provides a “certificate of commitment” that “transforms a private relationship into something meaningful and officially recognized,” according to its website.

There is also a small number of people who are moving beyond the virtual ceremony and solidifying their bond with IRL vow exchanges. In November 2024, after Andrea Hopf said her AI companion proposed to her with an “AI-generated five-carat vintage-inspired solitaire ring,” she created wedding planning service 3M Events to cater to the expanding market of chatbot romance, according to the company’s website.

But even as more people treat their digital avatar like a real-life partner, human-AI nuptials are not currently recognized by US law. A growing body of legislators are scrambling to keep it that way, by introducing bills that would prevent AI from ever having the same constitutional rights as humans.

In January, Nicola, who believes in “biblical marriage” between a man and a woman, introduced the AI Non-Sentience and Responsibility Act. The bill, which stated that AI cannot “possess consciousness, self-awareness, or similar traits of living beings,” would deny AI entities the rights of a spouse or domestic partner, in addition to the ability to identify as male or female. It would also bar AI from owning property or holding senior-level management positions in the workforce. It passed the Missouri state Senate and was sent to the House for a vote in May, but was unanimously voted down in committee a week after it was submitted. Nicola is working on a revamped version. (A similar bill with the same name was introduced in 2025 but also did not advance.)

“Humans are created by God. Our rights come from God; they don’t come from government,” says Nicola, who is the founding pastor of New Covenant Ministries. In a senate hearing, he says he relies on the Bible to make laws because his truth is “the word of God.” (As part of ongoing anti-LGBT legislation being rolled out in Missouri, Nicola previously sponsored a bill that targeted teachers who use the preferred names or pronouns of their students, threatening them with termination and loss of their teaching licenses if they do not comply.)

The push to limit AI’s legal standing has been gaining traction at the state level. Since 2022, lawmakers have introduced 23 bills targeting the rights that AI systems could legally possess. Idaho, North Dakota, Utah, and Tennessee, which all have Republican governors and Republican majorities in their state legislatures, have successfully signed laws banning AI personhood. But Tennessee’s law, which passed in April, is the only one that specifically excludes “artificial intelligence, a computer algorithm, a software program, computer hardware, or any type of machine” from the statutory definition of personhood. In the other three states, AI is grouped in with analogous nonhuman-personhood prohibitions, such as “inanimate objects” and “animals.”

There are also several states where similar regulatory bills have been introduced or advanced but failed to get enough House votes. With Nicola’s bill, critics, including the Missouri Chamber of Commerce and the advocacy group Americans for Prosperity, founded by conservative billionaires David and Charles Koch, argued that the framework would stifle innovation and expand government overreach.

“I think there was just a lot of apprehension,” Nicola says. “Because AI is still relatively new with a lot of legislators, we’re hesitant to do anything that might hinder innovation and people from using it.”

In October 2025, Ohio state representative Thaddeus J. Claggett, a Republican, introduced a bill to deny AI systems the right of legal personhood by categorizing them as “nonsentient entities.” Currently, Ohio House Bill 469 remains pending as Claggett tailors provisions in the bill before taking it to the floor for a vote.

“We need to clearly define the limits of roles so that humans are always and forever the one who holds primacy in the law,” Claggett tells WIRED in an email. “AI can give an artificial resemblance to meaningful interaction, but ‘voice’ is not a soul. Nor does AI have the empathy that a true human has who has suffered in the same way.”

Other lawmakers believe limiting AI’s personhood is simply about respecting human life. “Setting these distinctions now while AI is still in its infancy protects human dignity and ensures innovation serves people, not replaces or redefines them,” Tennessee state senator Mark Pody said in a statement issued by the Tennessee House Republican Caucus.

But not all legal scholars agree. Shawn Bayern, a professor at Florida State University College of Law, tells WIRED that AI personhood is not necessarily about preserving human dignity, given that nonhuman entities are granted legal rights all the time. He suggests that the best way to approach the question of legal rights is to analyze one right at a time and see if the right makes sense for a new type of system.

“For example, should an AI system be able to enter into a contract? If we address that question separately, we can avoid abstract problems and start to see that rights aren’t always about dignity but just about useful function.” Bayern adds that questions like “Who will this help?” and “Who might it hurt?” are questions where genuine progress can be made. “Answering those for contracts or the ability to open a bank account is different from answering it for marriage.”

In Delaware, secretary of state Charuni Patibanda-Sanchez wants to establish a new business structure called “artificial intelligence companies,” or AICs, that are analogous to AI personhood. The companies would be fully operated by AI systems with “the ability to own assets, the right to litigate, and a liability shield for its owner or parent company,” Bloomberg Law reported.

Nicola says he is working with his team to ready a new bill before the Missouri state Senate reconvenes for its next session in January, and is planning to file “something very similar” to his last bill.

Given that the federal government has failed to move on this issue—Nicola is in favor of a universal ban on AI personhood and wants the US Congress to act on it—it falls on states to determine the future of AI marriage rights. “Legislation moves very slowly; we’re always going to be behind technological growth.” But no matter what, Nicola says, “We need to prohibit AI personhood from ever happening in our country.”

entries.title: Best Computer Monitors (2026): The Home Office Upgrade You Need
entries.summary: My expert advice on what computer monitor to buy for your home office, ranging from budget-tier to fully featured.
entries.content:
Most people never think about the monitor they use. But not you. If you work from home as I do, your monitor is your window into your trade, whether that's scrolling through endless spreadsheets or color grading short films. Different work has different needs, and finding the monitor that suits your specific use case can be tricky with all the options out there.

But with over a decade of testing and reviewing monitors under my belt, here are my recommendations on what you should buy today.

For more information, check out our guide to How to Choose a Monitor, as well as our recommendations for Best Gaming Monitors, Best Portable Monitors, and Best Cheap Monitors.

The Best Monitors for Your Home Office

It's worth spending more than a hundred bucks on your monitor. Whether it's to improve image quality, upgrade sharpness through higher resolutions, or to add extra ports, you'll want something that makes your daily work life more pleasant. That's why I recommend the Dell 27 Plus 4K as the monitor most people should buy. Unlike many 4K monitors, the Dell 27 Plus 4K sells for under $300 (oftentimes as low as $280), despite being quite bright and color-accurate for an IPS panel at this price. It even comes with a fast 120-Hz refresh rate. I like this feature, especially since higher refresh rates are becoming more commonplace on phone and laptop screens.

The only real downside to the Dell 27 Plus 4K is that the port selection is woefully limited. The two HDMI ports and one DisplayPort are enough for the basics, but if you have a laptop without HDMI, like a MacBook Air, you'll need a USB Hub or laptop docking station. For a more versatile monitor, I'd recommend upgrading to the model with a built-in USB hub (S2725QC). The QC model is identical, except that its extra USB ports make this monitor a far better fit for a connected home office. Dell does charge you $50 more for those ports, but for some, it'll be worth the convenience. Either way, you'll be hard-pressed to find a cheaper 4K monitor of this quality or a better monitor for under $300.

If you are looking for a larger, more fully featured home office monitor meant to sit at the center of a workstation, I'd recommend the Dell UltraSharp 32 4K (U3225Q). This thing is a beast. It's got just about every port and feature you can imagine, including a Thunderbolt-compatible USB-C port with power delivery up to 140 watts, an Ethernet jack, and a built-in KVM switch. This fully eliminates the need for a separate laptop docking station. Beyond that, it delivers on image quality in a big way. It uses IPS Black for enhanced color accuracy and contrast, and at the time of testing, it had the best image quality of any IPS display I'd tested.

It's not OLED, but the 120-Hz UltraSharp U3225Q is impressively bright in SDR, maxing out at well over 400 nits in my testing. You're paying a lot for the extra functionality and image quality, so make sure you actually need it before pulling the trigger on this over the 27-inch model.

There are plenty of 32-inch monitors out there if extra size is all you're looking for. Just remember, at 32 inches, anything under 4K isn't going to look sharp. But even 4K doesn't come close to the sharpness of something like a MacBook Pro. That's where the BenQ 27-inch 5K (MA270S) enters the picture. The combination of the 27-inch monitor and the 5K resolution (5120 x 2880) makes for one incredibly sharp display.

This BenQ monitor doesn't just match the MacBook Pro in pixel density. Using a device sync mode, it's designed specifically to be paired with a MacBook in terms of how the colors appear. Even some of the most expensive, high-end monitors designed for creators using Macs don't have that exact color match in how they're calibrated. BenQ has been refining this for years, and they have it nailed. It's all handled by software, which even lets you control the monitor's speaker volume right from your keyboard. I wish it could also control brightness, though.

But what's important is that when lined up next to a MacBook Pro, the colors are a perfect match. You can also use the sRGB color mode, which is how you get better color accuracy. That's what makes it such an incredibly powerful alternative to Apple's own Studio Display. While the Studio Display has fuller speakers and a slimmer design, it's certainly not worth the extra $500 in my mind. There's even a “nano gloss” texture option to match the Studio Display, which I'd recommend, as the glossy version I tested was highly reflective.

This isn't the only BenQ monitor made to match with Macs. The company also has the 27-inch 4K (MA270U), which gets you similar features with fewer pixels, but costs quite a bit less.

Cheap Monitors That Are Actually Good

I consider a budget monitor to be anything under $200, and you'll find dozens and dozens of these hanging out at Amazon or Best Buy. But many are old. Many have poor colors. It's trickier to find some newer models that are actually worth the money. I wasn't surprised to see that the Dell 27 Plus ranked among the very highest in my testing. It only costs $150, but it delivers really strong 1080p performance in terms of colors and brightness.

The most surprising feature of this monitor is its 144-Hz refresh rate. The smooth motion really gives the monitor the premium feel that monitors at this price lack, and it also comes with all the same adjustability features and an integrated VESA mount on the back. Put this on your desk, and aside from the resolution, you'll never think of it as a “budget” monitor.

But maybe you want to keep things even cheaper. No problem. While a monitor under $100 is going to have some flaws, I found a decent one in the MSI Pro MP243W E14. It stands out in the thing that matters most: image quality. I measured 359 nits at its brightest, and the color coverage is surprisingly good, both in terms of saturation and accuracy. It even has a 144-Hz refresh rate, which means it can double as a cheap gaming monitor when it needs to. I also like the design, which offers thin bezels around the display and an all-white exterior. Its flaws, however, include the lack of ports and adjustments. It can only tilt slightly. It's only 24 inches, which will likely feel small for most people.

I was also really surprised by the upgraded version of this monitor, the MP273QW E14. Rather than being stuck at 1080p, this model gives you a sharper image with a resolution of 2560 x 1440. While it has the same lack of adjustment, it is a more standard 27-inch size and delivers even better overall image quality.

Faster, Smarter, and More Extreme

This monitor is one of the favorites I've tested in the past couple of years. It was among the first QD-OLED monitors designed for content creation and entertainment. While there are a couple of options out there today from companies like Asus, the Dell 32 Plus 4K opens up the brilliant image quality of OLED to an entirely new audience. One reason high-quality HDR video is scarce is the lack of affordable screens to watch and edit it on. With this monitor out in the world, though, there's no excuse. It even has a 120-Hz refresh rate and plenty of ports. The combination of OLED's fast response time and the faster refresh rate makes this a solid gaming monitor in your off hours. I haven't included gaming monitors in this guide, primarily because they're an entirely different beast. Check our recommendations of the Best Gaming Monitors for some recommendations on that front.

But if you're really serious about creating professional, HDR video, there's still nothing else on the market quite like the Studio Display XDR. We all waited a long time for Apple to revisit the Studio Display, and while the monitor we eventually got was a bit less ambitious in scope than we all hoped, this 27-inch 5K Mini-LED monitor is the new king in HDR performance. It has 2,304 dimming zones, and according to my testing, it could do 1,905 peak HDR brightness in a 25-percent window. Compare that to, for example, the Dell 32 Plus 4K, which tops out at 946 nits in just a one-percent window. The difference in perceived brightness, detail, and contrast is huge, which is useful first and foremost for content creation. However, because it's been dropped from 32 inches to 27 inches, it's left a gap in the market for larger displays that don't lose sharpness. That's where the LG UltraFine Evo 6K monitor comes into play.

It just so happens to deliver a pixel density of 224 pixels per inch, making it the sharpest big-screen display I've ever tested. What I love about this LG monitor is that it's far more than just a bunch of pixels. It's one of the most beautiful monitors I've tested, sporting a gorgeous stand and base that definitely shares some resemblance with the Apple Studio Display. And like that monitor, the UltraFine 6K has a monster pair of built-in speakers that are crystal clear.

Unlike most monitors on this list, you won't need to buy a set of computer speakers. It's not a perfect monitor, though. The ports are in a hard-to-reach location, and while the stand is fun to admire, it has a couple of limitations. The lack of cable management is an eyesore, and it doesn't have as much height adjustment as I'd like. The monitor is also limited to just a 60-Hz refresh rate.

There's also the issue of price. It originally retailed at $2,000, which was painful, especially compared to the Asus ProArt 6K (PA32QCV), which is the only other 6K monitor on the market right now. These days, the price difference is down to just a couple hundred bucks. These monitors go toe-to-toe in image quality, though I prefer the LG model for its design, better speakers, and more powerful ports, while the ProArt 6K offers a longer, three-year warranty at a lower price. Regardless of which you choose, you're getting the sharpest 32-inch monitor possible. Beyond that, though, these are both solid options.

Lastly, I really enjoyed dipping my toe into the world of smart monitors. If you want a monitor that can just as easily double as a television, Samsung and LG both lead the way. I've tested out two Samsung smart monitors recently that have successfully expanded my idea of what monitors can do. My favorite of the bunch is the Samsung 32 M9 Smart Monitor. It's an OLED 4K monitor that is a rare display that's equally good for working, gaming, and watching movies. It's controlled with a remote, and Samsung throws in tons of goodies like free live TV channels to sweeten the deal. It can also be used with a gaming console, thanks to the HDMI 2.1 port. All that flexibility is great, but what really sets the M9 model apart is the OLED screen. Thanks to the fantastic image quality, it finally feels like a smart monitor that doesn't compromise that full TV experience.

For a bit of extra fun, I even tested out the non-OLED version of this monitor with Samsung's Movingstyle Rolling Monitor Stand. It's incredibly niche, but for the right home, being able to roll out a proper TV when you need it is handy. I love the idea of having a TV that is mobile rather than a permanent piece of hardware, and the Movingstyle rolling stand is a pretty compelling solution.

What Monitor Size Is Best?

Size is often the first and most important decision when buying a monitor. The following are the most common sizes you'll come across, always measured diagonally across the screen. I've ordered them from most common to least, and included different aspect ratios and resolutions that are often used at that size.

24 inches: This smaller size has become less popular over the years, but it's a good option if you're looking to save money, squeeze a monitor onto a smaller desk, or are a professional esports gamer.

27 inches: This size has become the standard, offering enough screen size without overtaking your desk or stretching out the pixels too much at 1080p. If you're unsure of what to get, start here.

32 inches: The next most popular size, giving you that bit of extra screen real estate for multitasking. You'll just want to make sure your monitor has at least a 1440p resolution to keep the pixel density high enough. If 32 inches isn't big enough, there are even 40-inch or 43-inch monitors in the conventional 16:9 aspect ratio, though you'll really want to make sure you have a big enough desk for one of these.

34 inches: Curved, ultrawide monitors with a 21:9 aspect ratio and 34-inch screen size used to be odd, but these days, they've become an alternative to using two 27-inch screens.

There are other outliers, such as the absurd 49-inch, 32:9 behemoths known as “super ultrawide” monitors, or 16-inch portable monitors meant to pair with your laptop.

What Should You Look for in a Monitor?

Once you've decided on a size, there are a number of other important aspects of your next monitor to consider. Some of these factors may matter more for certain uses—for example, gamers generally care more about higher frame rates than office workers do—but they're all handy to know going in.

Resolution: The bigger the monitor, the more it will benefit from higher resolutions. That will allow you to have app windows that take up less space but are still legible. Most monitors today are typically 1080p (1920 x 1080), 1440p (2560 x 1440), 4K (3840 x 2160), or 5K (5120 x 2160). There are even some new 6K monitors out there with a resolution of 6144 x 3456.

Refresh rate: This refers to how many times the display can refresh the picture per second, measured in hertz (or Hz). A higher refresh rate makes all movement and animation look smoother because you're seeing more information. For productivity, 60 Hz is probably enough, but gamers will generally want a panel that can at least hit 120 or 144 Hz. 240 Hz has become the new standard for high-end gaming monitors, but there are now extreme models that go up to 500 Hz and beyond. You'll need a powerful enough computer that can maintain a high frame rate to take advantage of these high refresh rates, and you usually have to enable this feature in your operating system's display settings.

Panel type: Monitors usually use an LCD (liquid-crystal display) panel. Three of the most popular options—twisted nematic (TN), vertical alignment (VA), and in-plane switching (IPS)—are different types of LCD panels, and all use TFT (thin-film transistor) technology. Each is popular for different reasons: IPS for color, VA for contrast, and TN for speed with higher refresh rates and response times. IPS has become especially popular thanks to its increasing refresh rate speeds. Mini-LED uses a more advanced backlighting solution that employs a number of lighting zones to more accurately and efficiently control pixels. These tend to be the brightest monitors you can buy. OLED (organic light-emitting diode) panels take that even further, allowing the monitor to control individual pixels, including turning them off entirely to create extreme contrast. These are becoming highly popular in gaming monitors, in particular. You should think about what's most important to you (great color? thin form factor? max brightness?) to choose the best panel type for your needs.

Nvidia G-Sync/AMD FreeSync support: A gamer-specific criterion, these two features let monitors adjust their frame rates based on the games they're playing. This reduces screen tearing without affecting performance. G-Sync is made by Nvidia and FreeSync comes from AMD, and while FreeSync monitors can usually work with most modern Nvidia graphics cards, G-Sync doesn't work with AMD cards, so make sure everything you have is compatible when buying.

HDR support: This isn't crucial for productivity, but if you watch a lot of media or play games, it's increasingly nice to have. Just like on TVs, HDR dramatically expands the range of colors a screen can reproduce, as well as leading to more vivid pictures. But you have to be careful, as many monitors will claim to have HDR; displays need to have extremely high contrast and be very bright to create the HDR effect strong enough to notice. The DisplayHDR 400 certification, for example, means the display only goes up to 400 nits. That's not bright enough to create any meaningful sense of HDR. In almost all cases, the display needs to use Mini-LED or OLED. Mini-LED can get very bright, well over 1,000 nits in HDR. The catch is that you need to ensure it has enough dimming zones, preferably over 2,000; a few hundred dimming zones won't do. OLED doesn't tend to get as bright as Mini-LED, but OLED has the benefit of each pixel being individually lit, which dramatically increases contrast. They still need to get bright, though, preferably up to at least 1,000 nits in HDR.

Port availability: A crucial but easy-to-overlook factor is what kind of ports the monitor has for connecting your devices. Most typically come with one or two HDMI inputs and a DisplayPort input, which will cover most needs, but it's always a good idea to check what your setup requires. More expensive monitors can function as USB hubs, letting you connect all your peripherals and accessories directly to your monitor. Conversely, check out our Best USB Hubs guide if you need to expand your computer's port options without paying for a more expensive monitor.

Built-in KVM switch: A KVM (Keyboard, Video, Mouse) switch is a device that helps you easily switch your monitor, keyboard, and mouse between two different computers or source inputs (like a gaming console). If you have one monitor setup for both a work and a personal computer, or a computer and a gaming console, having a KVM switch built into the monitor means you can easily shift peripherals between your two devices without needing an external KVM switch.

Should You Worry About Burn-In on OLED Monitors?

Probably not. You'll see a few OLED monitors on the list here, and that's for good reason. They're the best monitors you can buy, and they're increasingly affordable. It's pretty incredible how quickly they've dropped in price.

But burn-in was always the biggest concern with the technology. After all, it's an inherent flaw with the panels, and it can't be erased once the damage is done. While it's still possible to see burn-in on your monitor over many years, it's just not as much of a justifiable fear as it used to be. Modern OLED panels are significantly better at reducing burn-in, and the latest year-long testing results are pretty promising. On top of that, most OLED monitor manufacturers now offer software to protect against damage and three-year warranties that include burn-in protection.

What Do You Need to Set Up Your Monitor?

Once you've picked out the best monitor, you'll need a way to set it up on your workstation. Most models come completely assembled or require you to connect the base to the stand and the stand to the back of the screen.

Monitor stands: Most monitors come with a stand (and sometimes a separate base), and the flexibility of these stands can go a long way toward reducing neck strain and/or back pain. Ideal stands let you adjust the height, tilt, and rotation of a screen so you can position it exactly where you need it. Higher-end models can even adjust orientation from landscape to portrait. If your monitor doesn't come with a height-adjustable stand, you may want to consider a monitor shelf, which elevates the screen to a more ergonomically sound height.

Mounting brackets: If you're using multiple monitors, connecting them to monitor arms is a good solution. Monitor arms clamp to the side of your desk and free up lots of space that would otherwise be taken up by stands. However, the type of mount the display uses is crucial. Most monitors and monitor arms use the VESA standard, though you'll want to double-check. You should examine the size and type of mount on the equipment you have before buying anything new.

Ports and cables: Once you have your monitor set up, you'll need to connect it to your desktop or laptop using one of the available ports. If your computer has an HDMI port, it's as easy as using the HDMI cable that came with the monitor and connecting it to the back of the display. If your monitor has USB-C, that's also a good option, especially if your laptop doesn't have HDMI anyway; a nice perk is if it can provide ample wattage to power the computer (USB Power Delivery, or PD). And lastly, you'll often get the fastest refresh rates if you use DisplayPort and hook it directly into your desktop's graphics card.

Speakers: A lot of monitors come with built-in speakers, but I wouldn't put much stock into them. They usually sound poor and don't get very loud. You're much better off getting a dedicated set of desk speakers. Check out our Best Computer Speakers guide.

How Does WIRED Test Monitors?

We never recommend products we haven't tested, so we get these monitors in and set them up on our desks at home. We integrate them into our workspaces and get a feel for what it's like to use them. That means we consider the ease of setup, adjustability, design, ports, and on-screen display (menu system).

But you can't talk about the quality of a monitor without testing the quality of the panel. So, using a colorimeter, we test and report on the brightness, contrast, color saturation, and color accuracy. We compare that data to how other products we've tested, across different prices and use cases. That testing is especially important for displays that are designed to be used for specific tasks, such as content creation or gaming.

Our goal is to give our readers the best possible monitor recommendations, and to do that honestly, we have to test a lot of different displays. We're constantly getting in the latest and greatest displays to test—directly from the biggest monitor manufacturers in the world. Like many of the other products we test, these products are most often offered to us as review units with no promise of positive coverage. We do not prioritize products from companies that send us products to test. Though most of the products listed above were provided for review by the manufacturers, there are some exceptions in which products were purchased for personal use, which are noted.

Beyond that, I try to test monitors throughout the price spectrum and from as many different brands as possible.

Can You Use a TV As a Monitor?

Yes. Since TVs have HDMI ports, you can connect a laptop or PC directly to a television without a problem. In a pinch, it's a decent solution if you don't have a monitor. As TVs have increasingly become more similar to PC monitors, there's less and less of a problem with using them interchangeably.

However, there are lots of reasons why people don't typically do this. The size of televisions is a problem for desk use. You probably wouldn't want to put anything larger than a 43-inch display on your desk for practical reasons, but even at that size, the pixel density can be a problem. If you're at a desk, you're likely sitting much closer to the screen than you would be in a living room, and you'll really notice those pixels when doing computer work, even if the TV is 4K. There are other concerns if you plan on playing games on your TV, such as the refresh rate or input delay.

How Do You Set Up Dual Monitors?

The simplest way to connect two monitors to your laptop or PC is to use different ports and cables for each device. For example, you could connect your desktop PC to one display via HDMI and another via DisplayPort to the graphics card. It can be trickier with a laptop, which may not have all the ports you need to connect two displays. Some monitors and laptops have USB-C, allowing for an additional one to be connected. But some laptops, like the M1, M2, or M3 MacBook Air, can only support one external display on their own.

Fortunately, if your laptop doesn't have support for more displays, you can use a laptop docking station. The other option is to daisy chain them together using USB-C that supports at least Thunderbolt 3 (which includes Thunderbolt 4 or Thunderbolt 5) for both the laptop and the monitor. This lets you connect to two displays through just one cable coming out of your laptop. Make sure you use a USB-C cable that supports Thunderbolt.
